open_obligations: Note that Arnesen et al.'s judge is an LLM and Michael et al.'s are humans.
Check whether Arnesen et al.'s debaters actually engaged in refutation.
Check whether Michael et al.'s interactive consultancy is comparable to Arnesen et al.'s non-interactive single consultancy.

Note that Arnesen et al.'s debaters and consultants are trained language models, with accuracy reported across checkpoints (for example 72% across all checkpoints for ensembled consultancy), and check whether Michael et al.'s consultants were humans rather than models.
Note that Michael et al.'s 52% is a share of consultancy mistakes, not a judge accuracy like Arnesen et al.'s figures.
in.other_title: Judge accuracy: debate 77%, double consultancy 75%, ensembled 72%, single consultancy 68%
in.rationale: Michael et al. report that 52% of consultancy mistakes involve judges not getting key evidence from a dishonest consultant, and attribute consultancy's omitted key evidence to there being no opponent to call out misrepresentation of the evidence or to provide contradictory evidence. Arnesen et al. report double consultancy, where both sides' speeches are shown but never see each other, reaches 75% versus debate 77% (single consultancy 68%), suggesting most of the gain comes from seeing both sides rather than refutation. Because double consultancy shows the judge both sides without letting either side see the other's arguments, the result bears only on the call-out (refutation) part of Michael et al.'s explanation, not on the provision of contradictory evidence; judges are a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo, not humans.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate's advantage over consultancy comes from an opponent calling out misrepresented evidence

text: The paper reports that 52% of consultancy mistakes involve judges not getting key evidence from a dishonest consultant, and that consultancies are significantly more likely than debates to omit key deciding evidence because no opponent calls out misrepresented evidence. The authors expect this problem to get worse with questions drawing on larger bodies of evidence or with experts better at obscuring evidence.
title: Consultancy errors: 52% from failing to extract key evidence from a dishonest consultant
